name: John J. Glessner House

documented_range.note: FROM: the family moved in in December 1887 (Glessner 1923; HABS data p. 1), and the February 1888 Inland Architect photograph shows the finished exterior; the day of the month is not stated, so the range opens on the 1st. TO: the research-centre conversion of September 1946 (HABS data p. 2) — stable door replaced, loft door closed up, courtyard paved — is the first exterior change recorded. The 1892 changes were interior. The phase is modelled as it stood on 1 July 1904, the scene date; values carried from the 1963-65 survey are ones the 1888 photograph brackets or the 1946 list does not touch (docs/RESEARCH/glessner_house_1904.md § 2).

placement.position_note: ON THE T-0474 PARCEL. data/street_grid/1904.json parcel prairie_1800 (Sanborn 1911 sheet 28) puts the lot's NE street corner at local E 1392.05, N -3217.24 and its NW rear corner at E 1338.07, N -3217.87. The house's north face stands on that 18th Street line and its east face 14.7 ft (4.481 m) behind the Prairie Avenue line — T-1731's reading of the same sheet at 6.0 px/ft, +/- 1.5 ft. Its NE corner is therefore E 1387.570, N -3217.292, and the footprint's origin (the SW corner of its bounding box) E 1338.687, N -3240.420. Rotation -0.669 degrees is the 18th Street line's own bearing (89.331 degrees, west to east) less 90, the long face's alignment. RECONCILED WITH THE PARCEL: the parcel is 177.1 ft deep, the house 161.25 ft plus the 14.7 ft setback, so the west face stands 0.35 m (1.16 ft) inside the parcel's alley line rather than on it; both readings carry more tolerance than that (+/- 1.5 ft on the setback, the parcel's own lines inferred), and the setback is kept because it is the one the street view depends on. Likewise the house's 74'-0" leaves 0.7 ft of the parcel's 74.7-ft frontage to the south of it. INFERRED for 1904: a 1911 map, carried back because the building did not move (1888 photograph; HABS 1963).
placement.symbolic_location: 1800 S. Prairie Avenue: the south-west corner of Prairie Avenue and E. 18th Street, on parcel prairie_1800 (data/street_grid/1904.json).

footprint.note: The ground-floor masonry outline, courtyard excluded: 34 points, about 7,054 sq ft, from HABS sheet 2's dimension strings (sheet 3 for the 99'-3" courtyard), checked against Sanborn 1911 sheet 28 (the house drawn as a stone courtyard plan with the coach house at the alley) and the 1888 photograph — T-1731's outline (data/research/glessner_house_1904_spec.json § footprint), converted from the building frame to metres: x = (161.25 - W) * 0.3048, y = (74 - S) * 0.3048. The courtyard projections (stair tower, hall bow, dining bay) are measured, +/- 0.5 ft; printed runs +/- 0.1 ft.

value.W: feet west of the Prairie Avenue (east) face
value.S: feet south of the E. 18th Street (north) face

frame_ft.note: THE BUILDING FRAME every other attribute here is written in: HABS IL-1015's own, the plans' frame with their north arrow pointing down the sheet. 161'-3" along 18th Street and 74'-0" on Prairie Avenue are printed on sheet 2. Heights are in feet above one of two datums, named with each value: `door` is sheet 6's '0.00 AT DOOR' (the front-door sill), and the sidewalk before the doorway is printed at -0.74, so a door-datum height stands 0.74 ft higher above the walk; `ng` is the grade sheet 4 draws at the 18th Street wall. generators/archetypes/masonry_house_params.py converts all of them to metres once, into the footprint's frame (origin at the SW corner of the house's bounding box, x east, y north).

grade_datum.note: Sheet 4's 18th Street grade is taken as level with the Prairie Avenue sidewalk (sheet 6's -0.74). The offset between the two datums is not measured by any sheet; T-1731 found them agreeing within about a foot where they overlap (the east wing's eave and ridge), and the committed heightfield is flat across the lot to 2 cm (e1871_postfire, 4.32-4.34 m), so the two grades are one ground here.

construction.note: Street walls of rock-faced granite ashlar in alternating high and low courses over brick (Glessner 1923; HABS data pp. 20-21, sheet 5); courtyard walls of common brick with limestone lintels and sills. THE STONE'S NAME IS DISPUTED and is carried, not resolved: 'Wellesley granite' (Glessner 1923; HABS 1963) against 'Braggville pink granite' (the museum, per the Prairie library dossier G02). Neither reading changes the geometry.

paint.note: Bare masonry: nothing records a painted or limewashed surface on the house, and the 1888 photograph shows the dressed stone itself. `stone` is the value renderers/web/js/facades.js reads as masonry (jitter only, no silvering).

roof_covering.note: Red baked terracotta tiles, unglazed (Glessner 1923), about 6 in wide with 5 in exposed (HABS data p. 21, 1963, when they had been tar-covered; the tar is later than 1904 and excluded). The ridges are crested with raised tiles at about 1.16 ft centres (sheet 6; the 1888 photograph), which the mesh draws as a plain ridge roll.

granite_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. v3's OWN READING of the same disputed evidence L295 records: Glessner 1923 and HABS 1963 call the stone 'Wellesley granite' (grey), the museum's own record calls it 'Braggville pink granite' (Prairie library dossier G02) -- T-1731 section 9 carries the disagreement UNRESOLVED. The default reads toward the grey name; v3 reads toward the pink one, since the museum's own naming of its own building is at least as good a witness as Glessner's 1923 memoir. Bounded the same way: the 1888 plate's monochrome pale tone, lifted toward pink rather than grey. Both are reconstructed; this is the comparison the owner asked for.

brick_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. Same attested fact as the default ('common brick of slightly pinkish colour', Glessner 1923) read with the granite's pink lean carried across, so the courtyard brick and the street granite (v3's own tint) sit closer in hue than the default's cooler grey granite against warm brick.

trim_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. Grey Joliet limestone (attested) a shade paler than the default's reading, to keep it legible against v3's warmer granite.

roof_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. 'Red baked terracotta tiles, unglazed' (Glessner 1923) states the family; v3 reads a brighter, less soot-dimmed red than the default, since nothing read actually states the tile had gone as dark as the default's value by 1904 -- both are reconstructed guesses at the same seventeen-year weathering.

copper_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. HABS 1963 records copper sheathing on the hall bow's roof; the default reads its 1904 state as soot-darkened bare copper, unpatinated. v3 reads it the other defensible way: copper in Chicago's coal-smoke air commonly shows early verdigris within a decade, so a bow roof seventeen years old is drawn beginning to green rather than staying brown. Neither reading rests on a source that states the 1904 colour; both are bounded by 'copper sheathing, weathered seventeen years.'

wood_tint.note: LINEAR rgb. Oak doors (c. 1888 photograph; HABS data p. 21); a lighter oiled-oak reading than the default's near-black value, since the c. 1888 photograph (monochrome) does not resolve a value this dark from a lighter one.

range_east_wing.note: The Prairie Avenue range: 74'-0" along Prairie by 26'-6" (sheet 2), two storeys over a raised basement with an attic under a steep N-S gable (Sanborn '2B'; sheets 4, 6). Street faces granite; its courtyard (west) face brick (sheet 2 hatching; Glessner 1923). The south face is drawn granite on the evidence of sheet 4's stipple — Sanborn prints 'WALL B.' inside it, recorded and not interpreted. Its west wall north of the north range's courtyard face is inside the house and is not drawn.

ridge_east_wing.note: Eave 27.1 ft and ridge 45.7 ft above the door datum are measured on sheet 6 (73.9 px/ft vertical, fixed by the sheet's printed 48.62 at the north chimney); the courtyard eave is 26.5 ft above north grade on sheet 4. INFERRED because the ridge LINE is placed on the wing's centre line (W 13.25): no roof plan confirms it, and the pitch that follows (about 55 degrees east, 56 west) depends on it. HABS data p. 21: 'steeply pitched, gabled roofs'. The 1888 photograph and HABS photograph 1 (1963) both show a symmetrical-reading gable end.

gable_east_wing_north.note: A stone parapet gable facing 18th Street, its coping rising from the eave corners to a chimney centred on the apex (1888 photograph; sheet 6 in profile; HABS photograph 1, 1963). The parapet's height above the roof (1.2 ft) is read off the 1888 plate against the eave, within about half a foot.

gable_east_wing_south.note: Sheet 4 draws the south gable edge-on in stipple (stone) rising to about ridge height, and sheet 6 draws its coping at the south end of the Prairie slope; so a parapet gable to match the north one. In 1904 the three-storey house at 1808 (Sanborn '3B') stood against most of it — that house is T-0475's, not drawn here.

range_north_range.note: The E. 18th Street range between the east wing (W 26.5) and the stable (W 125.75), 26'-10" deep (1'-7" + 4'-1" + 1'-8" + 18'-0" + 1'-6", sheet 2), two storeys over the basement (Sanborn '2B'). Granite to the street, brick to the courtyard. Its west end (about W 96.5-125.75) is the service block, entered 'through the great arch on Eighteenth Street' (Glessner 1923). The roof is drawn running into the east wing's and the stable's (to W 20 and W 139), under their slopes, so the valleys are the true intersections; its courtyard wall behind the hall bow is inside the house.

ridge_north_range.note: Sheet 4 (Section A-A, cut at W 51.3): ridge 34.1 ft above north grade, 14.6 ft south of the street face; street eave 23.1 ft, courtyard eave 26.5 ft; 36.6 degrees both ways, the courtyard slope flattening to about 27 degrees over its lowest 5.7 ft. The section is the only cut, and the profile is carried the length of the range on the evidence of the 1888 photograph (the 18th Street eave running level from the east gable to the stable's) and HABS photograph 1 (1963: one straight ridge from the east wing to the stable).

range_west_wing.note: The coach house — stable, carriage room, harness room and hay loft with the coachmen's rooms over — 35'-6" E-W by 59'-9" N-S at the alley (sheets 2-3), 1 1/2 storeys over the furnace room (Sanborn '1 1/2'; Glessner 1923: heating 'from the furnace room under the garage'). Granite on 18th Street and the alley; brick on its courtyard and south faces (sheet 2 hatching). ITS 1904 USE is inferred to be the stable it was built as: Glessner in 1923 writes 'the carriage house and stables (now garage)', and Sanborn labels it GARAGE in 1911, but nothing read dates the conversion before 1904. The exterior is the same either way.

ridge_west_wing.note: v3's OWN READING of HABS photograph 1 (Cervin Robinson, 1963), the same photograph the default reads. The source record itself claims only 'the stable's gable and ridge position and approximate heights' (data/sources/habs_glessner_photo_01_nw_1963.json) -- a single oblique 1963 web copy. The default reads the gable apex, the loft opening and the carriage doorway as standing on one photographed axis and puts the ridge at W 141 (the doorway's centre). v3 reads the same print more cautiously: a roofline running back from a gable does not have to track the doorway below it, so the ridge is kept on the wing's own geometric centreline (W 143.5, T-1731's original position) instead. The two eaves are read as one level (24.0 ft, the mean of the north range's attested street eave, 23.1, and its courtyard eave, 26.5) rather than importing two different neighbouring heights onto the two sides of one gable; ridge height follows from the reconstructed 45-degree pitch T-1731 originally bounded (36.6-54.5 degrees, the house's own two measured roofs). Carried to 1904 on the same grounds as the default: the 1946 list names no roof work and the 1888 photograph shows the same gable and turret.

gable_west_wing_north.note: A stone parapet gable on 18th Street with a relieving arch of radiating voussoirs over the loft opening (1888 photograph; HABS photograph 1). The coping stands about 1 ft above the roof line on the 1963 print.

gable_west_wing_south.note: Not drawn or photographed in anything read, as the default's note says. v3 gives it a parapet matching the attested north gable's form (parapet_ft 1.0) rather than a plain gable, because v3 reads the whole wing's roof as symmetric about its own centreline (see ridge_west_wing) and a symmetric roof reads more plausibly with matching gable ends than with one parapet and one plain wall. Equally undrawn either way. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

tower_stair.note: The round stair tower on the east wing's courtyard face: centre and radius measured on sheet 2 (+/- 0.5 ft), wall top 32.5 and cone apex 42.3 ft above north grade on sheet 4. HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923, the court) shows it: brick, conical roof, finial. The eave's half-foot overhang is the drawing's (sheet 4).

tower_north.note: Same sheet-4 heights the default reads (eave 32.9, apex 43.9 ft above north grade, S 0-16.7) and the same two photographs' form (a round granite drum, HABS photographs 1 and 13). v3's own reconstructed 'base' -- where the tower's granite drum begins, not drawn by any sheet -- is tied to the north range's own attested second-floor level (17.4 ft, T-1731 section 6) rather than the default's bare 20.0 ft, so the drum visibly rises from a floor line a visitor can already see elsewhere on the building instead of from an unremarked height.

tower_north_plan.note: Where in plan the tower stands is not drawn by any sheet, as the default's note says. v3's own reading of HABS photograph 1 scales the drum against the narrow corridor windows (about 0.8 ft glazed, Glessner 1923) visible beside it in the same frame, giving a smaller drum (6.5 ft radius) set slightly further from the east wing's face than the default's 7.35-ft reading. Bounded the same way: inside the cone's eave diameter the section fixes (16.7 ft) and tangent to the east wing's west face. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

hall_bow.note: The curved wall of the entrance hall in the inner NE corner of the courtyard: '9'-6" R' printed inside on sheet 2, centre measured, outer radius 10.1 ft; it sweeps from the east wing (S 37.6) to the north range (W 38.1). Sheet 3 draws it at the second floor with piers between large lights.

hall_bow_height.note: Two storeys to the courtyard eave (26.5 ft, sheet 4): sheet 4 draws the bow beyond its section plane with its wall top at the eave line, and HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923) shows it, brick with stone lintels and sills, three lights to a storey, rising to the eave of the east wing's courtyard slope. The light rows are the house's own first- and second-floor window heights (sheets 4-5).

hall_bow_roof.note: Same attested material as the default (HABS data p. 21: copper sheathing). Its form is not drawn; HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923) shows the bow's roof standing up as a distinct element between the two main slopes it joins, which v3 reads as a taller rise (4.5 ft) than the default's flatter 3.5-ft reading of the same oblique print, still well below the eaves it meets. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

bay_dining.note: The dining-room bay on the north range's courtyard face: five facets, 19.4 ft wide, projecting 10.3 ft (sheet 2; the room inside printed 17'-8" x 11'-0").

bay_dining_elevation.note: SETTLED IN FORM BY HABS PHOTOGRAPH 5 (a c. 1923 view of the court from The Story of a House), where T-1731 had a one-storey bay 'roofed below the second-floor windows' from sheet 3 alone. The photograph shows the bay as a masonry storey of large lights with a stone band at the second-floor level, over it a continuous glazed band of multi-pane sash, and a tall faceted roof of seamed sheet metal rising into the north range's slope. Sheet 3's light, many-sided outline at the second floor agrees: a glazed band drawn as joinery, not masonry. The HEIGHTS are read off the print against the adjoining wall's floor levels (sheet 4: second floor 17.4 ft), within about 1.5 ft: band top 23.0 ft; the faceted roof's point at the height of the north range's ridge (34.0 ft), where the print puts it, standing on the slope 6.8 ft behind the wall. Phase: a 1923 photograph, carried to 1904 because the 1892 changes were interior and nothing records exterior work before 1946. The roof metal is drawn in the copper slot; its material is not stated.

dormers.note: Three small pyramid-roofed dormers with finials on the east wing's courtyard slope (sheet 4: centres S 32.3, 45.0, 66.8; 4.4 ft wide; eave 32.9, apex 37.0 ft above north grade), one square light each. HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923) shows them. None on the Prairie slope (sheet 6; the 1888 photograph).

dormer_depth.note: How far the dormers stand forward on the slope is not drawn, as the default's note says. v3 reads a deeper dormer (5.1 ft front-to-back, nearer square against its 4.4-ft printed width) set a little lower on the slope (bottom 27.0 vs the default's 27.5 ft) than the default's shallower 4.2-ft reading. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

turret_stable.note: Form attested by the 1888 photograph and HABS photograph 1 (a small square louvred turret, pyramid roof, finial), as the default reads. v3 sets it on v3's own ridge line (W 143.5, see ridge_west_wing) rather than the default's doorway-axis ridge, and returns to T-1731's original reconstructed proportions (5-ft plan, 4-ft wall above the ridge, 5-ft pyramid, centred nearer the ridge's middle at S 20) instead of the default's photograph-scaled 6-ft turret set close to the gable at S 8 -- the same judgement call as ridge_west_wing, that a small print does not fix a turret's position along a 60-ft ridge to inferred-grade precision. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

chimneys.note: Four stone stacks. North gable: '48.62 +/- 0.02 AT TOP OF NORTH CHIMNEY' printed on sheet 6. South (12.85-16.81 ft north of the south end) and middle (base emerging 2 ft east of the ridge at 42.4 ft): sheet 6, tops measured. Great chimney behind the north gable: sheet 4 (S 16.5-20.5, top 46.6 ft above north grade); the 1888 photograph shows all four. N-S extents and tops only — see chimney_plans for the rest.

chimney_plans.note: The E-W size and position of every stack is not drawn, as the default's note says. v3 keeps the same centre positions the default derives from the ridge and the 1888 photograph (north gable and south on the ridge at W 13.25; middle 2 ft east of it) but reads each stack 3.4 ft deep rather than 4 ft, a plausible chimney breadth for a single flue rather than the default's slightly chunkier reading. The great chimney's position is reconstructed at the OTHER end of T-1731's own stated band (W 30-45): centred at W 34, near the band's west edge, against the default's W 40 near its east edge -- both are honest readings of the same open band. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

chimney_dining_room.note: Same evidence as the default: HABS photograph 1 shows a fifth stack on the north range's street slope 'near W 70', not listed in T-1731. The photograph's own record states it supplies only 'a chimney on the north range near W 70' -- v3 reads that approximate note as placing the stack a little further along the slope and a little lower than the default's box, within the same +/- 2 ft the default itself claims for this reading.

items.what: porte-cochere, closed by its two oak leaves
carved tympanum in a fan of radiating voussoirs
second-floor group of three, colonnettes between
carved string course under the group of four

openings_prairie.note: The Prairie Avenue front, opening for opening: sheet 6 (1965), confirmed by the 1888 photograph. Positions here are S (= 74 - d, the spec's feet north of the south end); heights above the door datum. The second-floor heads are the printed 24.30; the rest measured, +/- 0.3 ft horizontally and 0.5 ft vertically. The door's fan: tympanum radius 2.6 ft inside radiating voussoirs to 6.4 ft, springing at 9.3 ft (sheet 5). The porte-cochere is drawn closed by its oak leaves (the c. 1888 photograph; HABS data p. 21), their panels and straps not modelled — see porte_cochere_doors.

items.what: the great arch, over a recessed porch
wide window over the great arch
paired second-floor windows, east wing gable

openings_18th.note: No HABS elevation of 18th Street exists: positions are read as gaps in the granite on the first- and second-floor plans (sheets 2-3, +/- 0.4 ft). The great arch (12'-0" clear at 96'-6", sheet 2; springing 4.6, crown 10.8, voussoir ring 19 ft across, sheet 5) and the 12-ft window over it (20.0-23.7 ft, sheet 5) carry their own heights. HABS photograph 1 (1963) shows the same rhythm of narrow slit windows along the range. The 'narrow windows in its north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors' are Glessner's (1923). Items without a height take opening_heights.

items.what: first-floor window in the east wing's north face

openings_18th_photo.note: A first-floor window in the east wing's 18th Street face that the plan reading did not list: HABS photograph 13 (1965 photogrammetric plate, north elevation) shows two first-floor slit windows under the paired second-floor windows, at about W 4-5.6 and W 17.6-19.0 (scaled on the print against the 26'-6" gable, 34 px/ft).

items.what: loft opening over the carriage doorway, open in 1904
small windows flanking the loft opening

openings_18th_stable.note: Positions from sheet 3 (W 137.5-144.7; 132.4-133.6; 149.1-150.3). Heights read off HABS photograph 1 (1963) against the printed 12'-0" doorway: loft opening 17.4-24.4 ft, flanking lights 17.8-22.9 ft. HABS data p. 2 lists the loft door as 'closed up' in 1946, so it was an open loft door before; drawn as an opening.

items.what: the stable's carriage doorway, closed by two leaves

openings_stable_doors.note: The DOORWAY is attested: rectangular, 11.9-12.1 ft wide, 12.6 ft to the soffit of a single flat granite lintel (sheets 2, 5). The DOORS of 1904 are not known — HABS records the stable door replaced in 1946, and HABS photograph 1 shows the 1946 overhead door. Drawn as a pair of plain oak leaves filling the opening; the panel drawn carries the reconstructed grade because the leaves are ours. docs/LIBERTIES.md L295.

items.what: wide upper opening, a second candidate for a loft door

openings_alley.note: The stable's granite alley wall, openings read as gaps on sheets 2-3 (+/- 0.4 ft). No sheet draws their heights: see opening_heights.

items.what: windows under the eave over the underpass

openings_court.note: The east wing's courtyard face, read off sheet 4's elevation beyond the section plane (99 px/ft at full scale, read at 19.5 px/ft, +/- 1 ft; the sheet's horizontal origin is about 2.8 ft off the plan's, and positions are aligned to the stair tower the plan fixes) and checked against HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923). The underpass exit is 9.6 ft wide and 8.1 ft clear (sheet 4).

items.what: north range courtyard windows, narrow corridor lights, first floor
north range courtyard windows, narrow corridor lights, second floor

openings_court_north.note: T-1731 GAP 5: the north range's courtyard-face openings are not transcribed by anything read. The default reconstructs seven bays of paired room-sized windows; v3 reads this wall differently, as Glessner's own words describe it -- 'narrow windows in its north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors' (Glessner 1923) -- and carries that same narrow-corridor character across to the courtyard face of the same service range, six narrower openings rather than seven paired ones, thinned further at the second floor. Both readings are wholly reconstructed; neither sheet nor photograph shows this wall's openings. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

opening_heights.note: Heights for openings whose positions are read off plans. 18th Street: sheet 5 draws one pair of the narrow corridor windows beside the great arch (first floor 9.3-15.2, second 20.5-23.8 ft above grade), and those heights are applied to every narrow opening on the face — the spec called that step inferred; it is carried here at the grade of the weakest row this attribute also holds. The alley wall's ground-floor lights are set high, as stable lights are (7.0-10.5 ft), and its loft lights take the 17.8-22.9 ft HABS photograph 1 shows on the stable's 18th Street face. The north range's courtyard rows take the house's first- and second-floor window rows. docs/LIBERTIES.md L295. v3 reads the north range's courtyard windows narrower in height (10.0-13.0 ft first floor, 20.0-22.5 ft second) than the default's room-window heights, consistent with v3's narrow-corridor reading of that wall (openings_court_north). docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

eave_cornice.note: A moulded stone cornice under the Prairie Avenue eave and a plain eave course on 18th Street and the alley are visible in the 1888 photograph and HABS photograph 1; their depth and projection (0.5-0.7 ft) are ours. docs/LIBERTIES.md L295. v3 reads a shallower, plainer cornice projection (0.4-0.6 ft) than the default's 0.5-0.7 ft, equally unmeasured. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

courtyard_gate.note: The courtyard's entrance from the alley, 'through which the family moved in, unseen, in December 1887' (Glessner 1923): sheet 2 draws a pair of gate leaves at S 61.3-70.8 between a stub of the stable wall and a granite gate pier (S 70.8-74.8; drawn to the lot's 74.0).

courtyard_gate_heights.note: No sheet draws the gate or its pier in elevation, as the default's note says. v3 reads a lower gate (7.5 ft closed leaves) under a taller pier (10.0 ft) than the default's more even reading, still bounded by the underpass's attested 8.1-ft clear height at the other end of the same carriage way. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

courtyard_ground.note: Same evidence as the default: HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923, nineteen years late) shows a lawn and a hard drive from the underpass exit to the alley gate, and HABS data p. 2 dates the courtyard's paving to 1946, so before that it was not a paved lot. v3 reads a fresher lawn green and a more direct, less jogged drive line than the default's, and a paler gravel tone for the drive surface rather than the default's greyer concrete-like reading of the same 1923 print. Both are reconstructed for 1904 on the same photograph. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301.

porte_cochere_doors.value: two oak leaves, each three panels wide and six high, every square panel sunk in a circular moulding; a horizontal iron strap two rows up with a lock plate and two ring pulls; scroll-ended strap hinges
porte_cochere_doors.note: The c. 1888 photograph; HABS data p. 21 describes the same doors in a 1945 photograph. SIMPLIFIED in the mesh: the leaves are drawn as a flat oak panel with a centre joint (openings_prairie); the panels, mouldings and ironwork are not modelled.

front_door.value: heavily panelled oak with iron straps and a large square window behind an iron grille, under a stone lintel and a carved tympanum
front_door.note: Sheets 5-6; HABS data. SIMPLIFIED: drawn as a flat oak panel under a stone lintel and a plain tympanum inside the voussoir fan; the carving, grille and straps are not modelled.

vines.value: Boston ivy on the street fronts and Virginia creeper on the courtyard walls, planted 1887; their extent in 1904 unknown
vines.note: Glessner 1923 records both plantings in 1887. The 1888 photograph shows bare walls and HABS photograph 5 (c. 1923) shows bare stems on the courtyard's stair tower and bow. How far they had grown by 1904 is not recorded, and NO VINE IS DRAWN: the walls stand bare. docs/LIBERTIES.md L295.

ironwork_finish.note: Glessner 1923. The door straps, grilles and hinges it describes are not modelled (see porte_cochere_doors, front_door), so this is a statement about fabric no mesh surface carries.

function.note: The house of John Jacob Glessner (1843-1936) and Frances Macbeth Glessner, designed by H. H. Richardson and built by Norcross Brothers, 1886-1887; the family lived here from December 1887 (Glessner 1923; HABS data p. 1). The west wing was the family's stable and carriage house (see range_west_wing).

present_status.note: Verified 2026-09-30 on the museum's official history page. The 1946 endpoint belongs to this modeled exterior phase: conversion for the Lithographic Technical Foundation changed the building, not ended its existence. This present-day status does not extend the unchanged 1904 model through the present.

citations.citation: Glessner House, The House, section Preserving an Architectural Treasure. Read 30 September 2026.

what_it_supplies: the design of the porte-cochere doors and the form of the opening's corner stones, circa 1888
what_it_does_not_supply: dimensions (the opening is measured on HABS sheet 6)
the wood's finish or colour

research_note: AN INDEPENDENT VERSION OF THE GLESSNER HOUSE (T-1730), built from the same source set as the default (T-1732): T-1731's specification (docs/RESEARCH/glessner_house_1904.md, data/research/glessner_house_1904_spec.json), the HABS photographs (PR #169) and the Houghton Richardson drawings (PR #171). Every attested figure -- the footprint, the main ranges' eaves and ridges, the chimneys' measured positions and tops, the door and window tables, the materials as described -- is read the same way the default reads it, because those are direct HABS/Sanborn measurements and changing them would misrepresent the evidence rather than diverge from it. This version's independent reading is expressed at every attribute this project tiers inferred or reconstructed: the stable roof is kept symmetric on the wing's own centreline rather than shifted to the carriage doorway's axis (and tiered reconstructed rather than inferred, since a single oblique 1963 photograph is read here as too coarse to fix a 2.5-ft offset); the granite is read toward the museum's own 'pink' name rather than Glessner's 'Wellesley' grey, an explicitly unresolved disagreement in the sources; the north tower, the stable's ridge turret, the chimneys' depths, the dormers, the hall bow's roof, the courtyard-face windows and the courtyard ground are each reconstructed with different, independently bounded numbers. docs/LIBERTIES.md L301 records what v3 invents; L295 (the default's) is unchanged. Alternates for the owner's side-by-side comparison are under data/structures/versions/glessner_house/; the compare URL is /4d/dev/1904/?anchor=glessner_house&structure=glessner_house&version=v3. Interior out of scope, as for the default; the courtyard's south side (1808 Prairie's north wall, T-0475) is not drawn here either.
